destination.title: One banker was paid $550 million in a single year

short22: He was charged with ninety-eight counts — and pleaded guilty to six.
Michael Milken built the high-yield, or junk, bond market, financing companies the big banks shut out.
In 1987 his pay was reported near five hundred fifty million dollars — called the largest single-year pay in America.
After a cooperating witness pointed investigators his way, a 1989 indictment charged him with ninety-eight counts, including RICO racketeering.
But those were accusations — the case never went to trial.
In 1990 he pleaded guilty to six felony counts; the RICO charge and the other ninety-two were dropped.
He paid about six hundred million dollars and was barred from the industry for life.
In 2020 a presidential pardon forgave the punishment — but it did not erase the guilty plea, and did not lift that lifetime ban.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: There are a handful of people the world can never quite make up its mind about.
This is the story of how a kid from the suburbs of Los Angeles, working at a desk most Americans had never heard of, turned himself into the most powerful financier in the country.
And it is the story of a question that has never really been settled.
That was simply how the system worked, and almost nobody thought to ask whether it had to work that way.
Milken studied this same despised corner of the market as a young man, and he noticed something everyone else had filed away as obvious and never bothered to question.
If these bonds were a good deal for the people buying them, he could do something nobody else was willing to do.
Companies that could never have gotten a loan suddenly could.
In one single year, 1987, his pay was reported at around five hundred and fifty million dollars.
Almost nobody outside his own operation truly understood how it all fit together.
Wall Street had never watched anyone gather this much control over the flow of money this fast.
When you are the one who designed the game, and you are winning it by margins nobody has ever posted before, people stop asking how you got so good.
In 1986, the government found exactly that.
In 1986, Boesky was caught in a securities-fraud scandal of his own.
These were never going to be simple cases to make.
Then, in 1989, it landed with full force.
It had proven none of it, because the case never reached a jury.
In April of 1990, Michael Milken made a choice.
To one side, two years was a slap on the wrist, more proof that the powerful never really pay.
era_note: SET THIS. Modern stock footage is only usable if the case is modern; a 1960s case dressed in present-day footage reads wrong.

shorts.angle: One sheet of paper from his firm could put any company in America into play overnight.
shorts.type: C - the document that terrified every boardroom in the country
shorts.avoids: short22 covers the ninety-eight counts, the six-count plea and the pardon. It never explains the takeover machine, or the single letter that made a small raider dangerous to a giant.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Where in all of that did he stop bending the rules and start breaking them?
shorts.loop_join: L5 ends on the old rule being gone, and L1 opens by stating what that old rule was: to swallow a giant you had to already be one.

lines.text: In the old world, to swallow a giant company you had to already be a giant yourself. Milken changed the arithmetic.
source_lines: In the old world, if you wanted to swallow a giant company, you had to already be a giant yourself.
Milken changed the arithmetic.

lines.text: His firm perfected a single sheet of paper that could chill any boardroom in America. A letter saying Drexel was, in its own words, highly confident it could raise the money.
source_lines: His firm even perfected a single sheet of paper that could put a chill through any boardroom in America.
It was a letter stating that Drexel was, in its own words, "highly confident" it could raise the money for a given takeover.

lines.text: Not a guarantee. Just confidence. Yet coming from Milken, the market treated that letter as good as cash in hand.
source_lines: Not a guarantee. Just confidence. Yet coming from Milken, the market treated that letter as good as cash in hand.

lines.text: A corporate raider could wave it at a sleeping giant, and suddenly no company in the country felt too big to become a target.
source_lines: A corporate raider could wave it at a sleeping giant, and suddenly no company in the country felt too big to become a target.

lines.text: Over the decade the high-yield market swelled past a hundred billion dollars, and Milken was its undisputed king.
source_lines: Over the decade it swelled from a forgotten corner of finance into a market worth well over a hundred billion dollars, and Milken was its undisputed king.

lines.text: To raise serious money outside the old club, one road ran through Beverly Hills, through him.
source_lines: If you wanted to raise serious money outside the old club, there was one road, and it ran through Beverly Hills, through him.

lines.text: Chief executives who had felt untouchable watched their own stock the way you watch a storm rolling in.
source_lines: For generations, the largest corporations had seemed untouchable, too vast and too expensive for anyone to seriously threaten.
Chief executives watched their own stock the way you watch a storm rolling in.

lines.text: Supporters called it shaking the dust off lazy, bloated companies. Critics saw raids that buried companies under debt and cost ordinary people their jobs. Either way, the old rule was gone.
source_lines: Shaking the dust off lazy, bloated companies.

A wave of debt-fueled raids that buried great companies under mountains of borrowing, broke some of them apart for scrap, and cost ordinary people their jobs, all to enrich a handful of financiers standing in the middle.

shorts.angle: Weeks out of prison he was told he had months to live, and he is still here decades later.
shorts.type: B - the second act that made the verdict on him impossible
shorts.avoids: short22 runs from the indictment to the 2020 pardon. It never mentions the cancer diagnosis or the foundation, which is the whole reason people cannot agree about him.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: A record fine, a lifetime ban, and a presidential pardon. Which of those actually stuck?
shorts.loop_join: L5 points to a diagnosis as the start of the second answer, and L1 opens with that diagnosis, so the loop plays as the cause arriving right after the claim.

lines.text: Soon after his release, Milken was diagnosed with advanced prostate cancer. It had already spread. The prognosis he was reportedly given was measured in months.
source_lines: Soon after his release, Milken was diagnosed with advanced prostate cancer.
It had already spread.
The prognosis he was reportedly given was measured not in years, but in months.

lines.text: He founded what became the Prostate Cancer Foundation, the largest private funder of prostate cancer research in the world.
source_lines: He founded what became the Prostate Cancer Foundation, which grew into the largest private funder of prostate cancer research in the world.

lines.text: In a strange way it was the junk bond insight again. Find what the establishment has written off, and pour everything in.
source_lines: In a strange way, it was the junk-bond insight all over again.
Find the thing the establishment has written off, and pour everything into it.

lines.text: This time the payoff was measured not in money, but in years of human life. The cancer that was supposed to kill him in a year? Decades later, he is still alive.
source_lines: Only this time, the payoff was measured not in money, but in years of human life.
And the cancer that was supposed to kill him inside a year? Decades later, he is still alive.

lines.text: So which is the real Michael Milken? The felon who paid a record fine, or the philanthropist whose money extended countless lives? The second answer begins with a diagnosis.
source_lines: So which one is the real Michael Milken?
The felon who paid a record fine, or the philanthropist whose money has helped extend countless lives?
He is both, at the same time.
